intro:
These exercises build a single skill: choosing the smallest abstraction that solves a real duplication problem, and reaching for a macro only when syntax repetition is genuinely the thing being abstracted. The chapter frames the four mechanisms as a ladder you climb one rung at a time. Functions, generics, and traits cover variation in values, types, and behavior. Declarative macros cover small local syntax patterns. Procedural macros cover item-level generation. Build scripts and offline generators cover anything whose source of truth lives outside the crate.

The through-line is ordering. Macro expansion runs near the front of compilation, and every safety check you rely on runs on the output. A macro decides what code exists; it cannot decide what that code is allowed to do. Borrow checking, trait solving, and monomorphization all still happen after expansion. Keep that fact in front of you and most of the design questions answer themselves: if the friction is about ownership or types, a macro will not rescue it, and you have picked the wrong rung.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose function, generic, trait, macro, or build script honestly
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The honest way to classify these is to ask what the caller is actually passing: values, types, Rust items, or an external schema file. The answer to that question selects the tool, not habit.

Joining two labels into one string is a normal function. The caller passes two values and gets one value back. There is no repeated syntax to compress and no item to generate, so `fn route_label(service: &str, route: &str) -> String` is the whole job. A macro here would be pure overhead: a larger API surface to keep stable, worse diagnostics on a typo, and no expressive win, because the call already reads exactly like a function call.

Removing repeated route-table item syntax is the `macro_rules!` case. Here the duplication is in the syntax of the declarations themselves, which is precisely what the chapter's route-table example demonstrates. A declarative macro lets each route stay a compact line that expands to ordinary `Route` structs in a `Vec`. This is syntax abstraction: the variation is not in a value or a type but in the literal shape of the source the author has to type repeatedly.

Generating impls from a type annotation wants a derive or attribute procedural macro. The trigger is that code should attach to a type definition and emit trait impls for it. That is item-level generation over syntax the macro inspects at compile time, which is exactly what a proc macro does and a `macro_rules!` macro cannot do cleanly.

Mapping several concrete types through one algorithm is a generics or trait problem, not a macro problem at all. The variation is in the type, the behavior is identical, and that is the definition of parametric polymorphism. A generic function with a trait bound expresses it directly, gets full type checking, and produces clear error messages; a macro would only obscure that the real abstraction is over types.

Generating a client from an external API schema belongs in a build script or an offline generator. The source of truth is a file outside the crate, so the generation should run where that file can be read at build time and the output reviewed as ordinary Rust. A public macro call site is the wrong fit because the schema is not Rust syntax the caller types, it is external data, and binding generation to a macro invocation would couple the build to that data in a place the type system cannot help you reason about.
criteria: The label-joining case is assigned to a normal function, justified because there is no repeated syntax to compress and a macro only enlarges the API surface and degrades diagnostics.
Syntax abstraction (route-table repetition, declarative macro) is separated explicitly from type abstraction (mapping concrete types, generics or traits) and behavior abstraction.
The external API schema case is identified as a build-script or offline-generator job because the source of truth is an external file, not Rust syntax typed at a macro call site.

exerciseSolutions.title: Explain repetition and hygiene in a `macro_rules!` helper
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Read the chapter's `sum_values!` macro, since it has exactly the shape this exercise describes: a repeated list plus a local accumulator.

The repeated syntax pattern lives in the matcher fragment `$($value:expr),*` and its mirror in the expansion `$( total += $value; )*`. The `$( ... ),*` form on the matcher side says match zero or more comma-separated expressions; the `$( ... )*` form on the expansion side says emit the body once per matched expression. That repetition operator is part of the pattern grammar itself, not something applied afterward. It is what removes the repeated accumulator code at the call site: the author writes `sum_values!(1, 2, 3)` instead of three hand-written `total += ...` lines.

The local accumulator does not casually overwrite a caller variable of the same spelling because of macro hygiene. In operational terms: the identifier `total` that the macro introduces carries a different syntactic context, a different hygiene mark, from the `total` the caller wrote in `main`. The compiler treats those as two distinct names even though they are spelled identically. So when `main` has `let total = 40;` and the macro internally does `let mut total = 0;`, expansion produces two separate bindings that never alias. That is why the chapter's example can print `outer total = 40` unchanged after calling the macro. Hygiene is not the compiler vaguely handling it; it is a concrete identity rule that gives macro-introduced identifiers their own scope.

What still goes through normal checking is everything the expansion produces. Macros run near the front of the pipeline, but the Rust they emit is then handed to the same type checker and borrow checker as hand-written code. If `$value` were a `String` where `total` is an integer, the `total += $value` line would fail type checking after expansion, with the error pointing back through the span. Expansion decides what code exists; it does not exempt that code from type checking, trait solving, or borrow checking.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The `$( ),*` operator drives the repetition; hygiene keeps the macro's `total` distinct from the caller's, and the emitted `+=` is still type-checked.
criteria: The repetition form is identified concretely as `$($value:expr),*` on the matcher and `$( ... )*` on the expansion side, and named as part of the pattern grammar.

Hygiene is explained operationally: the macro's `total` carries a distinct syntactic context or hygiene mark, so it is a different name from the caller's identically spelled `total` and the two never alias.
The answer states that the expanded Rust is handed to the same type checker and borrow checker as hand-written code, with a concrete example of a post-expansion type error.

exerciseSolutions.title: Write a `macro_rules!` helper for repetitive checks
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The macro should accept several `name => bool` pairs and return how many of them are true. The matcher mirrors the chapter's list-shaped macros: a repetition over `$name:ident => $status:expr` with an optional trailing comma so the call site stays compact and editable.

The body is a single hygienic block. It declares a local accumulator `passed`, then uses the repetition operator to emit one conditional increment per pair, and finally evaluates to `passed`. Because the block ends in the accumulator expression, the whole `service_checks!(...)` invocation is itself an expression that yields the count, which is why the caller can write `let passed = service_checks!(...)`. The `$name` identifier is kept in the matcher to make the call site read like a labeled check list; the count logic only depends on `$status`, so the name is bound with `stringify!` to a discarded value purely for documentation. That keeps real business logic out of the macro: the macro contributes only the repetitive count pattern, not any runtime decision about what each check means.

This is the right scale for `macro_rules!`. The expansion is ordinary Rust, an integer accumulator and a few `if` statements, and the call site is plainly more readable than three or four hand-written increments. Nothing here reaches for procedural-macro power, because there is no item to generate and no type to inspect, only local syntax to compress.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The macro compresses repeated `name => bool` checks into one count; the expansion is a plain accumulator that the borrow and type checkers see normally.
criteria: The macro accepts repeated `name => bool` pairs via `$($name:ident => $status:expr),* $(,)?`.
The expansion counts true cases correctly by incrementing `passed` only when `$status` evaluates to true, returning 2 for the lab inputs.
Running the lab prints `passed = 2` and `total = 3`, matching the expected output.
The call site is a compact labeled list that is easier to read than three hand-written increment lines.

exerciseSolutions.title: Replace a useless macro with a normal function
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Neither macro abstracts any syntax, so both should disappear. The defect is the same in each case: a macro is being used where there is no repeated syntax to compress and no item to generate, which means the metaprogramming buys nothing and costs diagnostics and tooling quality.

`route_label!(service, route)` should become a normal function. It only expands to `format!("{}::{}", service, route)`, so the call already reads like a function call passing two values. Replacing it with `fn route_label(service: &str, route: &str) -> String` is strictly better: the signature documents the argument types, the IDE can autocomplete and show hover docs, go-to-definition lands on real code instead of a macro arm, and a wrong-type argument produces a precise error at the call site rather than an error inside an expansion. The macro form gave none of that and offered no syntactic win in return.

`retry_limit!()` should become a constant rather than a function. It only expands to a fixed integer, so it is a named value, not a computation. An associated constant such as `const RETRY_LIMIT: u32 = 5;` (or `RetryPolicy::RETRY_LIMIT`) expresses that intent directly: it has a type, it can be used in const contexts like array sizes and match patterns where a function call cannot, and it reads as a value at every use site. A macro that takes no arguments and returns a literal is a constant wearing a costume.

The refactor is justified on call-site honesty and tooling, not taste. A function call should be a function, and a named constant should be a `const`; making the API say what it actually is gives the reader accurate expectations, gives the compiler better error spans, and gives the editor real symbols to navigate. The trailing `!` was advertising metaprogramming that was never happening.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: A two-value transformation becomes a function; a fixed integer becomes a `const`, recovering typed signatures, const-context usability, and editor navigation.
criteria: `route_label!` is replaced with an ordinary function, justified by typed signature, precise call-site diagnostics, and working go-to-definition and autocomplete.
`retry_limit!()` is identified as clearer expressed as a `const` (or associated constant), usable in const contexts a function call cannot reach.
The justification is framed in terms of call-site honesty, diagnostics, and tooling rather than personal style.

exerciseSolutions.title: Sketch a derive macro API
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Sketch `#[derive(TopicKey)]` for the event types in a message-driven service. The job is type-local and concrete: given a struct or enum that represents an event, emit the routing key the platform uses to publish and subscribe, so that key derivation cannot drift from the type definition. A good derive does one type-local job well, and this is one.

Input item shape: the derive attaches to a `struct` or `enum` definition. For a struct it reads the type name and, optionally, designated fields; for an enum it can produce a per-variant key. The derive does not require any particular field layout, which keeps it usable on existing event types without restructuring them.

Helper attributes: support `#[topic(name = "...")]` at the type level to override the default key (otherwise the default is derived from the type's name, lowercased and dotted), and `#[topic(part)]` on individual fields to mark fields whose runtime values are appended to the static prefix to form a fully qualified key. Helper attributes stay optional so the common case needs only the bare derive.

Emitted code: the derive emits an `impl TopicKey for T` providing `const TOPIC_PREFIX: &'static str` (the static portion known at compile time) and a `fn topic_key(&self) -> String` method that concatenates the prefix with any `#[topic(part)]` field values at runtime. Naming the static prefix as an associated `const` lets call sites use it in const contexts and lets subscription tables be built without an instance.

Misuse diagnostic: if `#[topic(part)]` is placed on a field whose type does not implement `Display` (so it cannot be rendered into the key), the derive should emit a clear compile-time error on that field's span, something like `#[topic(part)] requires the field type to implement Display`. Reporting on the field span rather than the whole type makes the fix obvious. A second worthwhile diagnostic: reject `#[topic(name = ...)]` applied to an enum variant when it conflicts with a type-level name, rather than silently picking one.

The implementation lives in a separate proc-macro crate (`crate-name-derive`, declared with `proc-macro = true`), parsing the input with `syn` and emitting tokens with `quote`. The application crate re-exports the derive alongside the `TopicKey` trait so users see a single import. Committing to that crate boundary up front is part of the design: it is the cost the derive pays for being able to inspect and generate over the type's syntax.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Derive sketch: a type-level prefix as an associated const plus a runtime `topic_key`, with helper attributes for overrides and field parts.
criteria: A plausible derive name (`TopicKey`) and target item (event struct or enum) are described.
At least one emitted impl is specified concretely: `impl TopicKey` with a `TOPIC_PREFIX` associated const and a `topic_key` method.
Supporting helper attributes (`#[topic(name = ...)]`, `#[topic(part)]`) and a misuse diagnostic (`#[topic(part)]` on a non-Display field, reported on the field span) are named.
The answer acknowledges the implementation lives in a separate proc-macro crate using syn and quote.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose declarative macro, derive, attribute, function-like proc macro, or build script
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Each of the five concerns maps to exactly one tool, and the discipline is to give each tool one narrow job rather than forcing a single mechanism everywhere.

Repetitive integration tests want `macro_rules!`. The duplication is local repeated syntax, a fixed test scaffold instantiated over a list of cases, which is exactly the syntax-compression job declarative macros do best. A `test_cases!` macro that expands each `name => input => expected` line into a `#[test] fn` keeps the cases list-shaped and the emitted code ordinary. There is no item to inspect and no type to query, so reaching past `macro_rules!` would only enlarge the surface.

Event types that need codec impls want a derive macro. The code should attach directly to each type definition so the codec cannot drift from the fields, and it emits trait impls (`encode`/`decode`). That is the textbook derive case: `#[derive(Codec)]` on the struct, with the generated `impl Codec for T` living in a separate proc-macro crate.

Handler functions that need registration metadata want an attribute macro. Here an existing item, the handler `fn`, needs annotation-driven rewriting or registration: `#[handler(route = "/orders")]` can emit the original function unchanged plus registration glue (for example an inventory or linkme entry, or a generated registry function). An attribute macro is the right form because it receives and can rewrite the annotated item, which a derive cannot do to a free function.

The compact route-table DSL is the borderline case. As a small, fixed grammar it can stay a `macro_rules!` macro, exactly as the chapter's `routes!` example shows, expanding to a `Vec<Route>` of plain structs. If the grammar grows token-level constructs that `macro_rules!` cannot express cleanly, it graduates to a function-like proc macro such as `route_table! { ... }`, where token-level parsing is the real API. The honest choice depends on grammar size; the chapter notes that a much larger grammar tips toward a proc macro or an offline generator.

The API client generated from an external schema belongs in a build script or offline generator. The source of truth is a file outside the crate, so generation runs in `build.rs` (or a checked-in code generator) that reads the schema and writes Rust into `OUT_DIR`, included with `include!`. No macro form fits, because the input is external data, not Rust tokens the caller types.

Justifying one proc-macro and one non-macro choice operationally: the `#[derive(Codec)]` choice is right because the codec must stay attached to the type's field list and regenerate when fields change, which only type-attached generation guarantees; the build-script choice is right because binding schema-driven generation to a macro call site would couple the build to data the type system cannot reason about, whereas `build.rs` keeps the dependency on the schema file explicit and the output reviewable.

For testing and observability hooks: derive and attribute macros should ship `trybuild` compile-fail tests that assert the exact diagnostic for misuse (a missing required helper attribute, a wrong item kind), and the generated code should be covered by snapshot tests (for example `cargo expand` output checked into the repo or a `macrotest`-style snapshot) so a change in emitted code is reviewable in a diff rather than invisible. The build-script generator's output should likewise be snapshot-reviewed, and `cargo expand` remains the primary expansion-focused diagnostic when a macro misbehaves.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: One narrow job per tool: macro_rules! for repeated test syntax, derive for codec impls, attribute for handler registration, macro_rules!/proc-macro for the DSL, build.rs for schema-driven generation.
criteria: At least four distinct concerns are mapped to the correct tool: repetitive tests to macro_rules!, codec impls to a derive, handler registration to an attribute macro, the DSL to macro_rules! or a function-like proc macro, and the schema client to a build script.

One proc-macro choice (derive for codecs, justified by keeping generation attached to the type's fields) and one non-macro choice (build script, justified by an external source of truth) are defended operationally.
Testing and observability hooks are named: trybuild compile-fail tests, cargo-expand or snapshot tests over generated code, and expansion-focused diagnostics.

labSolution.explanation:
The lab fills in the `service_checks!` macro so it counts how many `name => bool` pairs are true. The matcher `$($name:ident => $status:expr),* $(,)?` accepts a comma-separated list of pairs with an optional trailing comma, which keeps the call site list-shaped and easy to edit. Each pair binds an identifier `$name` and a boolean expression `$status`.

The body is one hygienic block. It declares a local accumulator `passed`, then the repetition operator `$( ... )*` emits the conditional increment once per matched pair, so the macro expands to three `if` checks for the three inputs. The `$name` is bound to a discarded value via `stringify!` purely so the call site can read as a labeled check list; only `$status` drives the count. Because the block ends in `passed`, the whole `service_checks!(...)` invocation is an expression that yields the count, which is why `let passed = service_checks!(...)` works.

For the inputs `health => true`, `orders => true`, and `billing => false`, two statuses are true, so `passed` is 2. The program prints `passed = 2` and then the literal `total = 3`, matching the expected output exactly. The macro contributes only the repetitive count pattern; the emitted accumulator and conditionals are ordinary Rust that still pass type and borrow checking after expansion.

reviewAnswers.question: What operational difference separates `macro_rules!` from a procedural macro?
reviewAnswers.answer: A `macro_rules!` macro is a declarative pattern-matcher: it matches token patterns in its arms and expands to a substituted template, all expressed in Rust's macro grammar and compiled as part of the same crate. A procedural macro is an actual Rust function that runs at compile time, takes a `TokenStream` in and returns a `TokenStream` out, and therefore can run arbitrary logic to inspect and rewrite syntax. The operational consequences follow from that: proc macros must live in a separate crate marked `proc-macro = true`, add a compile-time dependency and a crate boundary, and can do item-level generation, whereas `macro_rules!` is lighter weight, stays in-crate, and is limited to template-style expansion of the patterns it can match.

reviewAnswers.question: Why do procedural macros operate on `TokenStream` instead of inferred types?
reviewAnswers.answer: Because of where they run in the pipeline. Macro expansion happens near the front of compilation, before name resolution, trait solving, and type inference, so there simply are no inferred types or resolved trait impls available to inspect yet. A proc macro therefore receives a `TokenStream`, a flat sequence of identifiers, literals, punctuation, and grouped sub-streams with spans, and must work purely from that syntax, typically parsing it with a library like `syn`. A direct consequence is that a macro cannot decide what to generate based on a field's concrete type or whether some trait is implemented, because that information does not exist at expansion time.

reviewAnswers.question: When is a derive macro the right fit instead of an attribute macro?
reviewAnswers.answer: A derive macro is right when the generated code should attach to a type definition and only add to it, typically emitting trait impls or helper methods, without modifying the type itself. An attribute macro is right when an item needs annotation-driven rewriting or registration, that is, when you need to transform or replace the annotated item, or attach behavior to functions, modules, or other items a derive cannot target. So derive fits codec, serialization, or builder impls on a struct or enum; an attribute macro fits decorating a handler function with routing metadata or rewriting a function's body. If you only need to add impls to a type, prefer derive, because it is the narrower and more conventional tool.

reviewAnswers.question: Why can a public macro be harder to evolve than a public function?
reviewAnswers.answer: A public function commits to a typed signature, so the compiler enforces the contract and refactors are guided by precise errors. A public macro instead commits to an input syntax grammar and an expansion, which is a much larger and looser surface: callers can depend on token shapes, on the exact names and items the expansion introduces, and on hygiene behavior, much of which is not captured by any type signature. Changing the grammar or the emitted code can silently break call sites in ways the type system will not flag at the macro boundary, and diagnostics for misuse are harder to keep good. That wider, less-checked contract is why a public macro is a heavier long-term commitment to keep stable than a public function.

reviewAnswers.question: What is one concrete signal that a normal function is better than a macro?
reviewAnswers.answer: The clearest signal is that the macro call already reads like a function call passing values, with no repeated syntax being compressed and no Rust items being generated. The chapter's `route_label!(service, route)` is the example: it just forwards two values to `format!`, so it should be `fn route_label(service: &str, route: &str) -> String`. When the only thing a macro does is take value arguments and return a value, a function gives you a typed signature, precise call-site diagnostics, and working editor navigation, while the macro adds API surface and worse errors for nothing in return.
